ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Paul Robeson

code.originalText: New patient visit for three months of low mood, exhaustion, poor sleep and withdrawal: depression screening, safety assessment and safety plan, tests for medical causes, and urgent psychiatric consultation

text.paragraph: New patient visit for three months of low mood, exhaustion, poor sleep and withdrawal: depression screening, safety assessment and safety plan, tests for medical causes, and urgent psychiatric consultation [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: He is exhausted, sleeps poorly and has lost the wish to sing, and wants to know what is wrong. [S]
He worries that a psychiatric record could be used against him by the people who have taken his passport and his work. [S]
He wants to keep working for civil rights and to sing again. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Paul Leroy Robeson was born on April 9, 1898, in Princeton, New Jersey. [D]
His father, the Rev. William Drew Robeson, was a minister, and his mother was Maria Louisa Bustill. [D]

In 1915 he was awarded a four-year academic scholarship to Rutgers, where he was elected to Phi Beta Kappa and graduated as valedictorian in 1919; he had been named to college All-America football teams. [D]
In 1923 he earned a law degree from Columbia Law School. [D]
In 1950 the State Department cancelled his passport, saying his overseas travel was 'contrary to the best interests of the United States'. [D]

He was blacklisted: his concerts were cancelled, record companies stopped recording him, his name was struck from the All-America teams and newsreel footage of him was destroyed, and his yearly income fell from more than $150,000 to less than $3,000. [D]

In 1956 he was called before the House Un-American Activities Committee, where he invoked the Fifth Amendment and closed by saying, 'You gentlemen belong with the Alien and Sedition Acts, and you are the nonpatriots, and you are the un-Americans, and you ought to be ashamed of yourselves.' [D]
His biographer Martin Duberman describes his first breakdown in 1955, after health problems related to prostate surgery: a period of intense, driven energy that was followed by a deep depression. [D]
A writer reviewing the Duberman biography has argued that he had the classic symptoms of bipolar disorder; no formal diagnosis of bipolar disorder in his lifetime is quoted. [R]

text.paragraph: 9 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

list.item: Concert singer and stage and film actor, trained in law, whose work has largely stopped: halls cancel his concerts, record companies will not record him, and he cannot travel abroad to perform because his passport is withheld; his income has fallen to a small fraction of what it was [S]
Speaks and writes for civil rights and against colonialism; was questioned by a congressional committee last year about his politics and travel [S]
Married; lives in an apartment in New York City; no firearm in the home [S]
Never smoked; an occasional glass of wine (AUDIT-C 1); no drug use [S]
Used to walk and swim most days; now rarely leaves the apartment [S]
Believes his telephone is listened to and that federal agents follow him; given the documented surveillance of people in his position, this is recorded as a realistic concern [S]
Supports he names: his music and the spirituals he grew up with, his work for civil rights, and old friends from the stage and the movement [S]

text.paragraph: No medications started by this date.

Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Tall, courteous and dignified; slowed movements and a quiet voice; mood 'worn through'; constricted affect; thought logical and goal-directed; no delusions or hallucinations; his account of being watched is consistent with the documented surveillance and is not treated as paranoia; insight and judgment good. PHQ-9 22 with item 9 scored 1: thoughts on several days that he would be better off dead, without intent or plan; no past suicide attempt; GAD-7 12; MoCA 28. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

code.displayName: Physical findings of General status Narrative

text.paragraph: Alert and engaged. Independent in daily activities; has stopped practicing and performing, reads little, and has turned down invitations to speak over the past two months. [S]

Vital signs recorded on 2026-03-09; see the Vital Signs section. Mental status: Tall, courteous and dignified; slowed movements and a quiet voice; mood 'worn through'; constricted affect; thought logical and goal-directed; no delusions or hallucinations; his account of being watched is consistent with the documented surveillance and is not treated as paranoia; insight and judgment good; PHQ-9 22 with item 9 scored 1: thoughts on several days that he would be better off dead, without intent or plan; no past suicide attempt; GAD-7 12; MoCA 28. The physical examination is limited to the findings relevant to this synthetic episode. [S]

Structured safety assessment: current ideation present, intent absent, plan absent, access to means reviewed: yes. Outpatient care with a psychiatric consultation in three days and close follow-up. C-SSRS screen: wish to be dead on several days in the past month; no active thoughts of suicide, intent, plan, preparation or past attempt. Risk factors reviewed: severe depression, an older man, insomnia, loss of work and income, isolation, and sustained persecution. Means counseling: there is no firearm in the home and he will not acquire one; medicines will be dispensed in limited supplies and kept in a locked box. A written safety plan was made with him, with warning signs, coping steps, people and places for distraction, and crisis numbers; the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) was saved in his phone. Safety is reviewed at every visit. [S]

S — Synthetic presenting problem at intake, superseded by the diagnosis at the psychiatric consultation; anchored to his documented depression and loss of work (D).
Sustained political persecution: passport withheld, concerts and recordings cancelled, income lost, and surveillance by federal agencies; a major and realistic stressor, not a delusion

value.displayName: Target of (perceived) adverse discrimination and persecution

list.item: About three months of low mood, exhaustion, poor sleep with waking at three in the morning, loss of interest in singing and reading, poor appetite with 5 kg weight loss, and withdrawal from friends, in a man of 58 under sustained political pressure; PHQ-9 22 with thoughts of being better off dead; depression suspected; medical causes being excluded and urgent psychiatric consultation arranged: active, confirmed [S]

Sustained political persecution: passport withheld, concerts and recordings cancelled, income lost, and surveillance by federal agencies; a major and realistic stressor, not a delusion: active, confirmed [S]

Evaluation: PHQ-9, GAD-7, AUDIT-C and a cognitive screen (MoCA); blood count, metabolic panel, calcium, TSH, vitamin B12, folate, morning testosterone and hemoglobin A1c, with HIV and syphilis tests, to exclude medical causes; a review of medicines; and a sleep apnea screen. Guideline: APA Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Depression Across Three Age Cohorts (2019); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026) [S]

Urgent psychiatric consultation in three days to confirm the diagnosis with a structured interview, screen for bipolar disorder, judge suicide risk and the level of care, and advise on psychotherapy, medicines, and when ECT or other treatments would be indicated. Guideline: APA Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Depression Across Three Age Cohorts (2019); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); The Practice of Electroconvulsive Therapy: Recommendations for Treatment, Training, and Privileging. A Task Force Report of the American Psychiatric Association, 2nd edition (record of the American Journal of Psychiatry review, 2002) (2001) [S]

Safety: structured suicide-risk assessment, a written safety plan, no firearm in the home, medicines dispensed in limited supplies and kept locked, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and a safety review at every visit. Guideline: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Major Depressive Disorder (2022); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024) [S]

Trust and equity: explain who can see his record and how it is protected; a therapist of his choosing, including a Black clinician if he wishes; treat discrimination and persecution as real stressors and record his account of surveillance as realistic; a social worker for help with income and costs; guard against the documented under-treatment of depression in Black patients by measuring response at every visit. Guideline: APA Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Depression Across Three Age Cohorts (2019); Williams DR, et al. Prevalence and distribution of major depressive disorder in African Americans, Caribbean blacks, and non-Hispanic whites: results from the National Survey of American Life. Arch Gen Psychiatry 2007;64(3):305-315 (2007); Sprenger S, et al. Retrospective Cohort Study of Racial-Ethnic Disparities in Receipt of Electroconvulsive Therapy, 2016-2021. Psychiatr Serv 2025;76(8):736-740 (2025); Racial disparities in psychotic disorder diagnosis: A review of empirical literature (2014) [S]
